chunks: He commanded it to remain stationary, submissive to His command,
He made its sun a clear sign for its day, and its moon a distinct sign from its night,
He set them in motion in the stages of their course, and ordained their travel in the steps of their ascent,
to distinguish between night and day by them, and to know the number of years and the calculation by their measures,
Then He hung in its firmament its Sky, and adorned it with its decoration, from the hidden pearls of its gems, and the lamps of its stars,
and He shot at the eavesdroppers with the shooting stars of its meteors,

and He set them in motion on the ease of their subjugation, from the stability of their fixed ones, and the movement of their wandering ones, their descent and ascent, their auspicious and inauspicious ones.

key_terms.ثَبَاتِ ثَابِتِهَا: the stability of the fixed stars
key_terms.ثَوَاقِبِ شُهُبِهَا: the shooting stars/meteors of its sky
key_terms.مُسْتَرِقِي السَّمْعِ: the eavesdroppers (jinn who listen to heaven)

ai.seo_question: How does Imam Ali describe the purpose and mechanism of the celestial bodies in Nahj al-Balagha?
ai.summary: In this passage from *Al-Ashbaah*, Imam Ali (peace be upon him) articulates the cosmic order (*nizam*) as a manifestation of divine precision, where celestial bodies serve both functional roles in timekeeping and aesthetic purposes as the 'jewelry' of the sky. This description aligns with the Shia scholarly emphasis on the rationality of creation, illustrating how the sun and moon are not merely lights but calibrated instruments for distinguishing day from night and calculating years. The mention of meteors (*thawaqib*) cast at eavesdropping jinn further connects the physical cosmos with the metaphysical realm, highlighting the continuous activity of the heavens in serving Allah's commands.
